final_proof:
Proof. Equip R^d with its standard inner product, defined for x = (x_1,...,x_d) and y = (y_1,...,y_d) by <x,y> = sum_{k=1}^d x_k y_k. Recall that a Hilbert-space basis (orthonormal basis) is an orthonormal set whose closed linear span is the whole Hilbert space.

For 1 <= i,j <= d, the standard vector e_i has i-th coordinate 1 and every other coordinate 0. Therefore

<e_i,e_j> = sum_{k=1}^d (e_i)_k (e_j)_k = delta_{ij},

where delta_{ij} is 1 if i=j and 0 otherwise. Thus each e_i has norm 1, and distinct e_i and e_j are orthogonal. Hence {e_1,...,e_d} is an orthonormal set.

It remains to prove completeness of this orthonormal set. Let x = (x_1,...,x_d) be any vector in R^d. Coordinate by coordinate,

x = sum_{i=1}^d x_i e_i.

Thus every vector in R^d belongs to span{e_1,...,e_d}. The reverse inclusion is immediate because every e_i lies in R^d, so span{e_1,...,e_d} = R^d. Consequently its closed linear span is also R^d.

Therefore {e_1,...,e_d} is an orthonormal set with closed linear span equal to R^d, and hence it is a basis for the Hilbert space R^d. QED.
